MSF issued the comments after DRC's government and the World Health Organization (WHO) had both spoken of signs of slowing transmission in some places earlier this week, prompting some relatively upbeat headlines and coverage. The outbreak, which was first declared in mid-May but likely started spreading several months earlier , is the largest in DRC's national history and the fastest-spreading on record anywhere. Did Ebola start spreading before officials even knew? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video What did MSF say about the outbreak and its spread? MSF — which has around 1,700 staff in the DRC, most of them Congolese — warned that while the observed spread was slowing in the initial epicenter of Ituri province, the number of new cases being recorded had not fallen on a national level. stories.title: East Africa: East Africa's Iconic Snow Peaks Face Imminent Extinction
stories.summary: East Africa's Iconic Snow Peaks Face Imminent Extinction Daily News FRESH snow covers Mount Kilimanjaro. 18 September 2026 Tanzania Daily News (Dar es Salaam) EAST Africa's iconic equatorial glaciers across three mountain peaks in Kenya, Uganda, and Tanzania will soon disappear entirely, with new climate assessments predicting total extinction within three to five years. According to the 2025 State of the Climate in Africa report, ice coverage on Mount Kenya Africa's second-highest peak has plummeted by 96 per cent over the past 115 years. The rapid retreat highlights a broader, unprecedented ecological shift affecting Mount Kilimanjaro in northern Tanzania and the Rwenzori Mountains situated on the border between Uganda and the Democratic Republic of Congo. Rainer Prinz, a climate scientist specializing in glacierclimate relationships, warns that the current rate of ice loss falls completely outside natural historical variations. " Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines During the past decade, we recorded a 40 to 60 per cent loss in East Africa's total glacier area meaning nearly half of the continent's equatorial ice melted in just ten years," Prinz explains, adding that while these glaciers may be as old as 10,000 years, the physical ice itself is considerably younger and rapidly disappearing. Contrary to popular belief, these high-altitude glaciers do not act as regional water towers or major reservoirs for surrounding populations.

Photograph: PEN International ‘We demand the truth’: Olga Tokarczuk and JM Coetzee lead calls for proof of life of disappeared Eritrean writers More than 180 writers sign letter renewing calls for information on 12 authors detained incommunicado since 2001 crackdown on free speech by Isaias Afwerki More than 180 writers have signed a letter to Eritrean president Isaias Afwerki calling for proof of life for 12 writers arrested in 2001. Nobel laureates Olga Tokarczuk and JM Coetzee join prominent writers including Colm Tóibín, Elif Shafak, Isabel Allende, Ben Okri, Yann Martel, Kamila Shamsie and Tsitsi Dangarembga in signing the letter organised by PEN International and dated 18 September, marking 25 years since a government crackdown on the independent press. “Within days, Eritrea’s free press and the nation’s independent voices were systematically crushed,” opens the letter. It lists 12 writers who have been held incommunicado since 2001, including the poet Amanuel Asrat and playwright and journalist Dawit Isaak. “The families of these writers, the Eritrean people and the global literary community have been met with a painful and unlawful silence,” continues the statement. “To withhold all information regarding their health, location, and survival is a violation of international law and an act of cruelty.” Along with Asrat and Isaak, the other writers named in the letter are Dawit Habtemichael, Fessehaye “Joshua” Yohannes, Mattewos Habteab, Medhanie Haile, Sahle “Wedi-ltay” Tsegazeab, Said Abdelkadir, Said Idris “Abu Are”, Seyoum Tsehaye, Temesgen Ghebreyesus and Yousif Mohammed Ali.

stories.title: ‘A map is never neutral’: meet the cartographers who took on centuries of western bias
stories.summary: ‘A map is never neutral’: meet the cartographers who took on centuries of western bias Equal Earth projection, adopted by the UN last week, provides an alternative to 16th-century Mercator display Three cartographers have spoken of their astonishment at the UN’s near-universal adoption of a map they created to more accurately show the sizes of Africa and Europe, even though they have received a few complaints from some disgruntled diplomats. The creators of the Equal Earth projection aimed to provide an alternative to the dominant 16th-century Mercator display, which critics have long faulted for giving the impression that northern hemisphere nations are larger than they are – and therefore subtly reinforcing perceptions of where global strength lies. “It has been a very busy week for me,” said Tom Patterson, a renowned US national parks cartographer who has had to virtually come out of retirement after being inundated with questions from governments on details of the new projection. The UN general assembly voted this month to adopt the new map , which more accurately represents the sizes of all continents, particularly Africa. It is hoped the projection will gradually replace Mercator on school walls and government websites. Put forward by Togo, the proposal was hugely successful, with 164 countries voting in favour.

stories.summary: Halima Kedir has lost count of how many trees she has planted. Some disparaged her efforts but now she says: ‘Those who tried to dissuade me are envious.’ Photograph: Amanuel Gebremedhin View image in fullscreen Halima Kedir has lost count of how many trees she has planted. Some disparaged her efforts but now she says: ‘Those who tried to dissuade me are envious.’ Photograph: Amanuel Gebremedhin Fifty billion trees by 2030: how Ethiopia is recruiting citizens across the country to plant, plant, plant After losing much of its forests in recent decades, the country’s people have led the way in planting saplings across the country as part of the government’s Green Legacy Initiative W hen Halima Kedir first began planting trees, she was met with scepticism and even mockery. “My neighbours discouraged me,” she recalls, sitting on a wooden chair in her garden, which is lush with the trees and fruits she has planted – banana, olive and grevillea among them. “They thought I was striving for nothing, but with time, many are realising that trees can be part of the solution to our problems as a way to fight climate change and food insecurity,” she says. Kedir, 35, who lives in the Berbere district of Ethiopia’s Oromia region, became an accidental environmentalist after planting thousands of trees – she has lost count of how many – inspiring others to follow suit. In a nation with a history of large-scale deforestation, Kedir’s work has not been easy.

"Korea is a long-standing and trusted partner of the African Development Bank. Our partnership now has the opportunity to enter a new phase, placing greater emphasis on investment, technology and private-sector engagement," said Dr Ould Tah , calling for increased mobilisation of Korean public and private capital alongside the Bank's financing. Deputy Prime Minister Koo Yun-cheol, who also serves as the Bank's Governor for Korea, praised the cooperation with the Bank over the years and reaffirmed Korea's commitment to deepen its economic engagement with Africa. The two leaders agreed to focus the next phase of cooperation on three priorities: AI and digital infrastructure, private-sector investment, and the development of industrial value chains across the continent. Korea, a member of the OECD's Development Assistance Committee, combines development cooperation with industrial capacity and private-sector innovation.

stories.title: Global Gender Gap Report: Women's hard-won gains 'fragile'
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5MeN4 Women make up less than a third of lawmakers in the US Congress Image: J. Scott Applewhite/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement The Global Gender Gap Report 2026, published by the World Economic Forum (WEF) on Wednesday, reveals that gender parity worldwide is closer than ever — standing at 69.2%. However, the Geneva-based nonprofit warned that full parity may still be 120 years away and that the progress made so far remains "fragile." The report, which looked at gender parity across workforce participation, education, health and politics in 145 economies, found that women now occupy senior leadership positions in government and business at levels that were rare globally when the index began in 2006. Yet, while women's presence at the top of politics has grown since the first report, the past decade has seen that trend reverse. The percentage of countries led by women peaked in 2022 and has now fallen back to 2016 levels.

As the US marks the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks launched by al-Qaida against targets in Washington and New York, the statistics underline the continued expansion of the veteran organisation in parts of Africa – in stark contrast with its relative weakness elsewhere. Compiled by Acled, which stands for Armed Conflict Location and Event Data, the statistics focus on the centre of Islamic militancy in three countries – Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger – which together comprise a huge and hotly contested zone at the heart of the strategic Sahel region.

stories.title: Slave-trade wealth was embedded in Britain’s financial system, research finds

Composite: Guardian/Diana Ejaita View image in fullscreen The scale of the financial system’s involvement in enslavement is greater than previously known or acknowledged. Composite: Guardian/Diana Ejaita Slave-trade wealth was embedded in Britain’s financial system, research finds Dozens of Bank of England directors and founding subscribers invested in trafficking of enslaved Africans The Bank of England and the British financial system were for centuries deeply involved in the enslavement and transatlantic trafficking of millions of African people, according to new research on Britain’s slavery history. Research by historians compiling the Register of British Slave Traders has found that the scale of the financial system’s involvement in enslavement is greater than previously known or acknowledged. The Bank of England, the central bank owned by the government since nationalisation by Clement Attlee’s Labour administration in 1946, had dozens of financiers involved in its foundation who were also significant investors in the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans.

stories.title: More than 1,000 women invested in companies at heart of Britain’s slave trade

Composite: Guardian/Palesa Monareng More than 1,000 women invested in companies at heart of Britain’s slave trade Women used profits from trafficking of enslaved Africans to secure their families’ futures, research reveals More than 1,000 women invested in the slave trade, challenging the conventional notion that they were passive beneficiaries and largely fought for its abolition. Researchers found women bought, sold and brokered shares in the Royal African Company, South Sea Company, and other separate ventures, and used profits from the trafficking of enslaved Africans to secure financial independence and provide for their families. By the time the RAC, which trafficked about 150,000 enslaved people, was dissolved in 1752, women made up about 10% of shareholders.

stories.title: The London hospital funded by donors who invested in the slave trade
stories.summary: Illustrations by Diana Ejaita The London hospital funded by donors who invested in the slave trade Barts is one of many UK institutions whose benefactors were involved in the trafficking of enslaved Africans Inside the Great Hall of St Bartholomew’s North Wing, alongside stately portraits of the apostle from whom London’s oldest hospital takes its name and King Henry VIII, extravagant commemorative boards adorn the walls. The Great Hall was a grand, formal space where governors weighed their philanthropic donations and drafted their wills, many while investing in the stock of companies built on the trafficking of enslaved Africans. Today, many of those donors are commemorated in acrylic gold paint on the boards. The Register of British Slave Traders , a joint venture between Lancaster University, the University of Manchester and University College London, includes biographical data on every known investor in Britain’s transatlantic trafficking of enslaved African people from the 16th to 19th centuries. It reveals how wealthy individuals , often enriched by the proceeds from racialised chattel enslavement, donated to hundreds of church parishes and helped to fund schools, hospitals and charities across the country.

stories.title: 'It's like a dog set loose on us' - fear over Kenya's crackdown on foreign traders
stories.summary: Image source, BBC/Brian Khisa Image caption, Burundian tuk-tuk driver Ndaikech Ali says Kenya, which has been so welcoming to him for years, now feels hostile By Basillioh Rukanga Published 12 September 2026 For Ndaikech Ali, who has been traversing the streets of the Kenyan capital eking out a living as a tuk-tuk driver for the past nine years, Nairobi's traffic - not xenophobia - has been his biggest concern. During his time in the East African nation, the Burundian says he has always found Kenyans to be friendly and welcoming - that is until last week, when the president ordered a crackdown on foreigners working as traders or operating small-scale businesses. "Now they have turned against us," he told the BBC at the Burundian embassy in Nairobi where many have been queuing this week for documents to allow them to travel back home. "The threats are manyâ¦ even from children," he said, adding: "It's a like a dog has been set loose upon us. We have been bitten." President William Ruto made his remarks last week when addressing Kenyan traders gathered at state house - in reference to legislation before parliament that seeks to exclude foreign nationals from petty trade and to mandate the local sourcing of certain materials. During his speech, he said that all foreign nationals operating small businesses had until 7 September to pack up shop, saying such low-level jobs should be reserved for Kenyans. Ali, like others, panicked, saying it seemed the president's announcement had been interpreted by some Kenyans as a signal that foreign nationals were no longer welcome in the country. "We face harassment and can't work," he says. "If our work is stopped, we lose the income that enables us to pay rent and buy food.
